text: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
picture: The Storyteller, holding a dim red lantern low, stands in a dark hollow with mist swirling around his boots. Far behind him, the faint, foggy outline of a lone motel, with one window glowing.

text: I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between two towns that don't talk to each other.
picture: Exterior night shot: a small, run-down single-storey motel sits in thick fog. An empty two-lane road stretches past it. One window in the front office glows faintly. The rest is dark and indistinct.

text: Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
picture: The motel's row of identical doors seen through fog. Dim yellow bulbs barely light the walkway. The doors are closed and still.

text: The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in ink is a promise.
picture: Mr. Pell stands behind the worn counter, smiling faintly down at the open guest book. Dawn light from the window catches his glasses cord. He holds a fountain pen, admiring it, his expression suggesting conviction.

text: Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at two fourteen a.m. A different name every night.
picture: June stands at the counter in dim morning light. One finger rests under a single, freshly written line of vivid red ink in the open guest book. A ring of keys is in her other hand.

text: Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
picture: Close-up on dark green door number six under a dim yellow sconce bulb, nailed shut with weathered grey planks against the cinder-block wall as thick fog presses in.

text: The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I started watching.
picture: June sits rigid at the front desk, both hands clutching her phone. The open guest book lies before her, its red ink hidden. Blackness fills the window behind her. Her face is pale, alert, and hollow with fatigue.

text: Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
picture: A wide view of the motel office from the inside. June is a small, tense figure at the desk. Outside the window, the parking lot's sodium lights strobe and gutter, throwing sickly orange pulses across the dark room.

text: At two fourteen, the pen moved.
picture: An extreme close insert on the surface of the guest book. A dark wood fountain pen lies at a slight, unnatural angle, as if nudged. The desk lamp light is dim and unsteady, casting long, trembling shadows. No hand is seen.

text: Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
picture: Close on June's face. It's lit only by the cold blue glow of her phone screen. Her eyes are wide, staring fixedly at the phone, refusing to look down. Her jaw is tight with dread.

text: I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
picture: June's phone screen in a low-angle shot. On the screen is a grainy black-and-white security feed view. It shows the back of June's head as she sits at the desk. The rest of the dim office stretches out behind her.

text: And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
picture: The same phone screen, viewed from behind June's shoulder. The grainy CCTV image shows the back of her head and, directly behind her, the top of a tall, thin, hooded figure in a dark, dripping raincoat. It is bent slightly forward.

text: man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
picture: A wide 'CCTV' view from the high corner of the office. June sits at the desk. Directly behind her, the tall, skeletal figure in the dripping dark raincoat bends over her shoulder, its hooded face aimed down at the guest book, one pale hand reaching for the pen.

text: I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
picture: An extreme close-up on June's face from the front, frozen. Her eyes are wide with raw terror, glistening with unshed tears, staring straight ahead. A single drop of water falls from above, tracing a cold line down her cheek.

text: When the lights came back, the office was empty.
picture: The motel office at night, lit by a buzzing fluorescent overhead. The counter is cluttered, one desk lamp fallen over, June's empty chair twisted away from it. The entire room is stark and vacant.

text: The book was open. The ink was still wet.
picture: Close-up on the open guest book. An empty line at the top. A single, wet drop of dark red ink is just starting to bleed into the paper below it.
sound: the faint ticking of a wall clock

text: Room six. Two fourteen a.m. And the name was mine.
picture: Extreme close-up on the now-written-in line in the guest book. The name 'June Marsh' is written in a flowing, unfamiliar script in bright red ink. 'Room 6' and '2:14 AM' are written neatly beside it.

text: Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
picture: Mr. Pell leans over the motel counter under bright morning light, peering through his reading glasses at the open guest book. His lips are pressed into a thin, somber line, deeply focused on the page.

text: Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
picture: Mr. Pell reaches towards an old, dark wooden board covered in hooks behind the counter. He selects a large, tarnished brass key on a red plastic tag from an otherwise empty hook. His expression is grim.
sound: the jingle of a lone key

text: "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."
picture: Mr. Pell extends the brass key across the counter towards the foreground. His face is kind but etched with a deep, weary sadness. June's hand is a blur in the extreme foreground, hesitating to take it.

text: The Wayside Motel is still open. The night desk is always staffed. And if you sign the book, check the name above yours.
picture: The Storyteller stands in his misty hollow, lowering his red lantern. Far in the distance, shrouded in thick fog, is the silhouette of the deserted motel strip. One door with boards is faintly outlined, a dim, sickly yellow light leaking from behind the wooden slats.
